wa_bears_breast_mountain_southwest_face.notes: ~1,000 ft up the left-hand of two parallel gullies NE of Dutch Miller Gap; continuous 3rd-4th class scrambling on ledges and short steps; the gully narrows and steepens about 1/3 of the way up.
Above the constriction, angle eases to a distinctive 'white fan' of chunky rock, then traverse right across heather and broken rock to the ridge crest at the second notch NW of the summit block.
Steep, slightly bulging rock; crux with marginal protection near an old, loose piton and broken rock. Ends at a roomy belay ledge.
20-ft crack/dihedral using stemming and heel-toe jams, into a 20-ft squeeze chimney.
Moderately inclined crack on solid rock with dramatic exposure to the true summit.

wa_chianti_spire_east_face.notes: Flakes and a crack lead up into the route's obvious wide dihedral; the easier right-hand start (wider crack) joins here, while the harder left-start finger-crack variation (5.10b, with a chimney exit) rejoins by the top of this pitch. Protects well despite the width.

Short fist crack widens into true offwidth; using face holds outside the crack makes it feel easier than it looks from below. Belay from a stance on a horizontal break (parties on the harder left-start variation rate this pitch 5.9+/10b).
Easier face-and-flake climbing up a lower-angle dihedral; a slung block provides a natural belay. Strong parties often link this with pitch 2 as one long block.
Cracks lead to a balancy, low-friction blind step left across an arete, protected by a single fixed bolt, gaining a sloping stance below the steep splitter above.

The technical crux: a sustained, steep thin-hands crack widening through cupped hands to fists, capped by a short strenuous offwidth move, to a bolted belay stance that doubles as a rappel anchor. Bring doubles from #0.75 to #3.5 to cover the full size range.

Continues the same crack system through wide hands and offwidth in a shallow dihedral, then a rising ramp trends left to the base of the exposed summit block. Watch for rope drag/snag risk through the wider sections.
Short, exposed final moves on good holds gain the summit block, passing a single fixed bolt that also serves as the first of four double-rope rappel anchors used to descend the route.

wa_direct_north_buttress.notes: From the toe of the buttress, go right up slabs, then trend left into a broken slabby wall seamed with cracks. Climb the cracks to a recessed belay. The rock low on the buttress is poor in places; the couloir to the left is the loose, rockfall-prone alternative this start avoids.

Climb the crack in the dihedral to a roof. The crack widens toward the roof; stay in it until below the roof, then move out right, where a good hold helps. Pull through to a small ledge belay. A #4 cam is the piece that makes this pitch comfortable.
Continue up the corner system to the base of a chimney, then climb the chimney system; the two pitches can be linked. Stacked flakes lead into the chimney, so test before weighting.

Traverse left past loose blocks, which is the most unpleasant ground on the route, then back right through thin cracks with sparse protection. Ledge systems and easy but poorly protected ground follow. Protect the follower on the traverses and keep the rope clear of loose blocks.

Climb the ridge toward the snow patch; the rock here is often wet from melt. Beyond the snow, climb the face behind it by a left-hand crack to join the original 1967 North Buttress line. Crampons are recommended and a light axe helps for the snow.
A strenuous left-facing corner with a crack running from hands to fists, steep and sustained for much of a long pitch. The rock quality improves markedly from here up. Bring wide hand and fist sizes.
Two pitches up the buttress crest to the ledge at the base of the offwidth, where the 1967 party bivouacked.

16a climbs the offwidth, awkward with a pack, past some fixed gear; it is graded from 5.10a to 5.10-. 16b is the bypass: start up the offwidth, then trend right around the corner onto easier ground at about 5.8 and belay above the wide section.
Climb the buttress crest on steep, airy face holds with big exposure. Belay below the long crack system above.
A long series of thin cracks, close to a full rope length, to a small stance. The rock here is lichen-covered; expect it to feel harder when damp.

Easier blocky ground up the buttress to the ridgeline. Many parties leave the rope here and move up Class 4 and easy 5th, trending right to the summit ridge. Descend west on Class 3-4 ground, then snow and cliff bands back to camp.
